entries.note: Brits often say sea where Americans say ocean; the word comes from Greek Okeanos, the world-encircling river of early Greek cosmology.
A very old Germanic word for any large body of water; its German relative See means both sea, as in Ostsee, and lake.
The top ocean zone; the pelagic element means of the sea or of the open sea.
The name of the middle layer of the ocean, built on the same pelagic element as [[epipelagic]].
The dark, deep zone of the ocean; the bathy- element simply means deep.
The name of an even darker ocean zone; it means bottomless, as you can guess from [[abyss]].
The deepest (hadal) zone, named from the same root as [[Hades]], the underworld.
Shares an Indo-European ancestor with Latin [[piscis]]; it once meant any sea creature, and its Old English and Middle English plural was fishes.
Uses the old broad sense of [[fish]]; originally just cuttle, possibly related to Germanic words for pocket or scrotum, like the cod in [[codpiece]].
Not a fish; the name reflects the older meaning of [[fish]] as any sea-dwelling animal.
Not a fish; it is called one because of the older meaning of [[fish]] as any sea creature.
A Germanic word for big sea creatures, found in [[walrus]]; once spelled hw-, like what, where and when, before the letters were swapped.
Old English had horse whale; confusion with a Scandinavian walrus word reversed the parts, so the name means whale horse.
The walrus's scientific name: Odobenus means tooth walker, and rosmarus comes from Old Norse for walrus, literally horse whale, like [[walrus]].
The Old Norse name for Orkney's Mainland (also called Pomona), with the same horse element as in [[Odobenus rosmarus|rosmarus]].
Probably corpse whale, from its mottled grey look under the surface; an alternative links it to knal, needle, because of its tusk.
The narwhal's scientific name; fitting, as its tusk is really a tooth.
The whale order, from a Greek word for sea monster; Ceto was a primordial Greek sea goddess who gave birth to monsters.
The division of [[Cetacea]] made up of the baleen whales, such as humpbacks.
The toothed whales, which include dolphins, porpoises, orcas and sperm whales, so dolphins technically are whales.
Etymologically a pig fish: French for pork and poisson (fish) squashed together, with a syllable lost from each.
The Old English name for porpoises, sea pigs, referring to their rounded snouts and stocky bodies, like [[porpoise]].
From Greek delphis, womb, probably because they give birth to live young, though possibly because of their shape.
From Latin dorsum, the back, which is a handy way to remember where the dorsal fin is.
They were said to be originally called whale killers because they hunt baleen whales; the hosts debate whether it is really a whale or a dolphin.
From the same root as Tolkien's [[orc]]; the genus name Orcinus is related to Orcus, the Roman god of the underworld.
Long used in English for large deadly sea creatures; Tolkien drew on the Old English sense of a big scary thing, sharing a root with [[orca]].
The orca's former scientific name, either calling it combative or drawing directly on [[gladiator]], swordsman, from the Latin for sword.
Named because the waxy [[spermaceti]] in its head, used for focusing sound and buoyancy, looks like sperm.
The waxy substance in a [[sperm whale]]'s head, prized by whalers; its name means sperm of the whale.
A self-explanatory name, referring to the big bumpy part of its back.
Self-explanatory, as the whale looks a bit blue; its scientific name [[Balaenoptera musculus]] is more interesting.
The blue whale's scientific name: Balaenoptera means winged whale, and musculus, related to muscular, comes from a word meaning mouse.
Another sea mouse: the same word as [[muscle]], spelled differently, both meaning little mouse, perhaps because mussels resemble little mice stuck to things.
The same word as [[mussel]], meaning little mouse; a rippling muscle supposedly looks like a mouse crawling under the skin.
The humpback's scientific name; the -ptera element is the same as in [[helicopter]] and [[pterodactyl]], referring to long wing-like fins.
Origin unknown; entered English with Hawkins's specimen exhibited in 1569. Shark already meant scoundrel in the 1400s, perhaps the animal's namesake, cf. [[sea attorney]].
Old English lacked a general [[shark]] word, using specific names like houndfish or sea dogs, which survive as dogfish.
The name for hammerhead sharks until the 1740s.
A word for [[shark]] borrowed from French and Spanish, presumably after encounters in the Caribbean.
Sailors' name for the brown shark, quoted from Melville's Mardi; it supports the idea that [[shark]] the animal was named after the human swindler.
Origin unknown; possibly a sailors' variant of [[squirt]], since squid squirt.
From Latin calamus, reed or pen, because squid squirt ink and are pen-shaped; unrelated to the calli- of [[calligraphy]].
Its calli- element means nice and, despite appearances, is not related to [[calamari]].
Means head foot; the hosts discuss whether to pronounce it with a k or s sound, as with encephalitis.
Octopuses, octopodes and octopi are debated; the word only existed in modern Latin, and -i follows [[polypus]] but is the wrong Latin declension.
The ancient Greek word for an octopus, commonly pluralised polypi in English, which gives some precedent for octopi.
Its cod means scrotum, not the fish, and potentially relates to the cuttle of [[cuttlefish]].
The fish might be named after the cod meaning scrotum, as in [[codpiece]], making it a possible ball sack of the sea.
The genus name of cuttlefish, and also the brown pigment once made from their ink.
Means sailor; early bestiaries described it floating with arms spread like sails, perhaps an image from the [[argonaut]]; the ship is probably named after it.
Named after the [[barnacle goose]], thought to hatch from it; possibly from bare neck, more likely French bernac influenced by hibernacule.
Originally just barnacle, a goose said to grow on waterside trees from a shell; goose was added to distinguish it from the shellfish [[barnacle]].
Covered in a previous episode; clam literally means to constrict, clinch, pinch or cramp, which is just what a clam does.
Doesn't need to invoke the shellfish, since [[clam]] itself means to constrict or clinch.
Related to words for shell and bone, such as osteo-, and to a word for shell or potsherd, so related to [[ostracize]].
From an ancient Greek vote on exile in which names were written on pot shards, related to [[oyster]].
A town in southern France, Rob's wife's hometown, thought to be named after the [[oyster|oysters]] found off its coast.
From the Greek word for nettle, because these animals are often stingy; the group includes jellyfish, anemones and corals.
Another fish that isn't a fish, from the old broad use of [[fish]].
Means daughter of the wind, from the Greek for wind, which is related to Latin [[animus]]; the idea is movement.
A device for measuring wind, named from the same Greek word for wind as [[anemone]].
Sea cucumbers' group; the name can mean spiky skin or hedgehog skin, linked to Greek echinos, hedgehog, and possibly [[echidna]].
Greek echidna meant snake or viper, so it is unclear why a hedgehog-like animal got the name; the link to [[echinoderm]] is uncertain.
Named because a land [[urchin]] was a hedgehog, just as Greek echinos meant both hedgehog and sea urchin.
The French for [[sea urchin]]; it is the same word as hérisson, hedgehog, taken from different stages of the word's development.
Calling a Victorian child an urchin probably compares them to a hedgehog, a lost little spiky animal, rather than to a [[sea urchin]].
A German scientific coinage based on a Greek word, used in German texts for all kinds of tiny organisms, eggs and larvae.
Combines proto-, early or original, with the Greek word for animal also seen in [[zoo]] and [[zodiac]].
The hosts debate the plural and settle on amoebas, while suggesting that amoebae also works.
Simply a Norwegian word for tiny shrimp, one of many fishing words borrowed through contact between Norwegian and English sailors.
Probably came via Spanish from Taino baracuta, a solitary person or animal, perhaps mixed with a Spanish word meaning overlapping tooth or snaggletooth.
Came to English from Spanish, which took it from Arabic, from Latin, from Greek; the root probably means to dart or rush.
From French, from Latin platessa, meaning flat, because it is a flatfish; fish-and-chip shops love puns on it, such as Fred's plaice.
The had- part is unknown; -ock is the diminutive suffix of [[buttock]], [[bullock]] and [[hillock]], so a had was bigger than a haddock.
Possibly a diminutive of a word meaning army, from their schooling; the -ing suffix means associated with, as in [[Viking]].
Discussed in an earlier episode: vic means bay or camp, and -ing means the people of, the suffix that also appears in [[herring]].
Meant spear in Old English, matching the fish's long spear-like nose; the same gar appears in Beowulf's first line, in Spear-Danes.
Usually said to come from [[Sardinia]], but Aristotle's mention makes that doubtful; they may share a sard- element, possibly the other way round.
Discussed in an earlier episode; its relation to [[Cyprus]] is murky, and it's hard to tell which is named after which.
Its link with [[Cyprus]] is really messy: unclear whether copper is named after the island or the island after copper.
The Old English word, with cognates including Latin anguilla, meaning little snake or serpent.
Not actually a true [[eel]], but a member of a completely different order.
A fish whose name uses sarcastic in its root sense of flesh-tearing, as in [[sarcasm]], for its large mouth with scary teeth.
A shaggy-lipped [[carpet shark]]; tasselled refers to the shaggy bits, and wobbegong is said to be an Australian Aboriginal word meaning shaggy beard.
So called because their patterns can resemble ornately patterned carpets.
Believed to be named after the speed of its movements.

entries.translation: triggerfish with a snout like a pig
entries.note: The Hawaiian name of the reef [[triggerfish]]; its repeated syllables reflect how Hawaiian doubles words to intensify them.
